stem: A 35-year-old patient presents with a well-demarcated, erythematous plaque covered with silvery scales on the extensor surface of the elbow. During examination, gentle removal of the scales results in tiny pinpoint bleeding spots. This clinical finding supports the most likely diagnosis. Which of the following signs is being demonstrated?
stemHtml: Q 02: A 35-year-old patient presents with a well-demarcated, erythematous plaque covered with silvery scales on the extensor surface of the elbow. During examination, gentle removal of the scales results in tiny pinpoint bleeding spots. This clinical finding supports the most likely diagnosis. Which of the following signs is being demonstrated? (Question Id: 515018)
keywords: Silvery scales – Suggests psoriasis, a chronic plaque type.
Extensor surface – Classic location for chronic plaque psoriasis.
Pinpoint bleeding after scale removal – Directly points to Auspitz sign, confirming psoriasis.
The combination of well-demarcated erythematous plaque + silvery scales + pinpoint bleeding (Auspitz sign) is the high-yield feature cluster for psoriasis.
keywordsHtml:
1. Silvery scales – Suggests psoriasis, a chronic plaque type.
  2. Extensor surface – Classic location for chronic plaque psoriasis.
  3. Pinpoint bleeding after scale removal – Directly points to Auspitz sign, confirming psoriasis.
The combination of well-demarcated erythematous plaque + silvery scales + pinpoint bleeding (Auspitz sign) is the high-yield feature cluster for psoriasis.

C.title: Auspitz sign
C.body:
Auspitz sign: This is the appearance of pinpoint bleeding when psoriatic scales are scraped off.
It occurs due to the thinning of the suprapapillary epidermis over elongated dermal papillae containing dilated capillaries in psoriasis.
This sign is highly suggestive of psoriasis and is used to confirm the clinical diagnosis.
Additional note: The sign reflects epidermal-dermal microvascular changes in chronic plaque psoriasis.
C.bodyHtml:
• Auspitz sign: This is the appearance of pinpoint bleeding when psoriatic scales are scraped off.
  • It occurs due to the thinning of the suprapapillary epidermis over elongated dermal papillae containing dilated capillaries in psoriasis.
  • This sign is highly suggestive of psoriasis and is used to confirm the clinical diagnosis.
  • Additional note: The sign reflects epidermal-dermal microvascular changes in chronic plaque psoriasis.

A.title: Koebner phenomenon
A.body:
Appearance of psoriatic or other skin lesions at sites of trauma.
Not the same as bleeding upon scale removal; it is lesion induction after injury.
A.bodyHtml:
• Appearance of psoriatic or other skin lesions at sites of trauma.
  • Not the same as bleeding upon scale removal; it is lesion induction after injury.

B.title: Nikolsky sign
B.body:
Gentle lateral pressure on skin causes the epidermis to shear off.
Seen in pemphigus vulgaris and other blistering disorders, not psoriasis.
B.bodyHtml:
• Gentle lateral pressure on skin causes the epidermis to shear off.
  • Seen in pemphigus vulgaris and other blistering disorders, not psoriasis.

D.title: Darier sign
D.body:
Rubbing a lesion causes urtication and redness.
Seen in mastocytosis, not psoriasis.
D.bodyHtml:
• Rubbing a lesion causes urtication and redness.
  • Seen in mastocytosis, not psoriasis.

E.title: Wickham striae
E.body:
Fine, lacy white lines on mucosal surfaces.
Characteristic of lichen planus, not psoriasis.
E.bodyHtml:
• Fine, lacy white lines on mucosal surfaces.
  • Characteristic of lichen planus, not psoriasis.

keyConcept: Auspitz sign is pinpoint bleeding after removal of psoriatic scales, caused by dilated capillaries under a thin epidermis. It helps clinically confirm chronic plaque psoriasis.
keyConceptHtml: Auspitz sign is pinpoint bleeding after removal of psoriatic scales, caused by dilated capillaries under a thin epidermis. It helps clinically confirm chronic plaque psoriasis.

cells: Definition

Chronic,
immune-mediated skin disorder characterized by well-demarcated erythematous plaques with silvery scales
Most common type of psoriasis (~80–90% cases)
cellsHtml:
• Chronic,
  • immune-mediated skin disorder characterized by well-demarcated erythematous plaques with silvery scales

cells: Typical Sites

Extensor surfaces (elbows, knees),
scalp,
sacral area
Helps in clinical recognition and diagnosis
Lesion Morphology

Erythematous, raised plaques with silvery-white scales;
Auspitz sign may be present
Key diagnostic feature for physical examination
cellsHtml:
• Erythematous, raised plaques with silvery-white scales;
  • Auspitz sign may be present

cells: Pathophysiology
Dysregulated T-cell mediated inflammation → keratinocyte hyperproliferation and angiogenesis
Explains rationale for immunomodulatory treatment
cellsHtml: • Dysregulated T-cell mediated inflammation → keratinocyte hyperproliferation and angiogenesis

cells: Trigger Factors

Stress,
infections (e.g., streptococcal),
trauma (Koebner phenomenon),
drugs
Guides prevention and patient counseling
Associated Findings

Nail changes (pitting, onycholysis),
arthritis (psoriatic arthritis)
Important for systemic evaluation
Management Overview

Topical corticosteroids,
vitamin D analogues,
phototherapy, s
ystemic agents (methotrexate, biologics)
Stepwise treatment based on severity and extent
cellsHtml:
• Topical corticosteroids,
  • vitamin D analogues,
  • phototherapy, s
  • ystemic agents (methotrexate, biologics)
Stepwise treatment based on severity and extent

tables.heading: Differential Diagnosis of Chronic Plaque Psoriasis

cells: Eczema (Chronic Atopic/Dermatitis)

Itchy, ill-defined erythematous plaques;
lichenification common
cellsHtml:
• Usually more pruritic, less well-demarcated;
  • scales are not silvery;
  • Auspitz sign absent

cells: Lichen Planus

Violaceous, flat-topped, polygonal papules;
Wickham striae on mucosa

Color (violaceous),
mucosal involvement,
Wickham striae present,
no Auspitz sign
cellsHtml:
• Violaceous, flat-topped, polygonal papules;
  • Wickham striae on mucosa

cells: Tinea Corporis (Fungal Infection)

Annular plaques with central clearing, active borders;
scaling

Fungal hyphae on KOH,
central clearing,
less sharply demarcated
cellsHtml:
• Annular plaques with central clearing, active borders;
  • scaling

• Fungal hyphae on KOH,
  • central clearing,
  • less sharply demarcated

cells: Seborrheic Dermatitis

Greasy, yellowish scales;
commonly scalp, nasolabial folds

Greasy yellow scales,
distribution differs,
less well-demarcated,
Auspitz sign absent
cellsHtml:
• Greasy yellow scales,
  • distribution differs,
  • less well-demarcated,
  • Auspitz sign absent

cells: Pityriasis Rubra Pilaris

Follicular papules,
orange-red plaques with islands of sparing

Follicular involvement,
“islands of sparing”,
less common,
histology differs
cellsHtml:
• Follicular papules,
  • orange-red plaques with islands of sparing

cells: Cutaneous T-cell Lymphoma (Patch Stage)

Erythematous patches/plaques with scaling,
chronic course

Progressive,
patchy,
often asymmetrical,
biopsy shows atypical lymphocytes,
no Auspitz sign
cellsHtml:
• Progressive,
  • patchy,
  • often asymmetrical,
  • biopsy shows atypical lymphocytes,
  • no Auspitz sign

diagrams.heading: Psoriasis – Chronic Plaque Psoriasis
diagrams.description: The diagram provides a comprehensive, medical graduate-level overview of chronic plaque psoriasis. It illustrates a typical scaly plaque on the elbow, highlighting the Auspitz sign (pinpoint bleeding after scale removal). It also shows common sites of involvement (scalp, knees, lower back), triggers (stress, infections, trauma, medications), nail changes (pitting, onycholysis), and psoriatic arthritis features. This visual is designed to help identify key clinical features, sites, and systemic associations of chronic plaque psoriasis for diagnosis.
